h1: Zappa hops and their odd mix of mint and passion fruit
title: Zappa Hops: Mint and Passion Fruit | Craft Beer School
desc: Zappa hops for homebrewers: the odd mix of mint and passion fruit, how to test a strange hop with a split batch and a 20 litre pale ale plan.
teaser: Mint and passion fruit sound like a cocktail, not a hop. Zappa is one of the strange ones. Strange hops are worth learning slowly.
standfirst: Zappa is sold on a surprising pair of aromas: mint and passion fruit. A hop like that can make a memorable beer or a confusing one. This guide shows how to test it safely in a 20 litre pale ale and what to pair it with.
sections: A hop that does not behave

Most hop descriptions agree on citrus, pine and tropical fruit. Zappa is described with passion fruit and mint, which is a less common pairing. Mint and menthol-like notes come from certain terpenes in the oil. Passion fruit often tracks with sulphur-containing thiols, the same family that gives some hops and wines their tropical, boxwood edge.

That mix is why the hop is fun and why it can go wrong. Too little and it vanishes. Too much and the beer tastes like toothpaste. The right amount depends on your base beer, your water and your yeast, so expect to brew it more than once. We do not quote an alpha figure here. Take it from the lot's certificate of analysis.

A single hop beer is the cleanest way to meet a hop. Keep the base plain so the hop is the only story. For 20 litres at OG 1.046:

  • Pale ale malt 3.6 kg (90%).
  • Wheat malt 0.4 kg (10%).

Mash at 66 °C for 60 minutes. Ferment with a clean American ale yeast at 18 to 19 °C. With an FG of 1.010, the beer lands at about 4.7% ABV from (1.046 - 1.010) x 131.25. Aim for 25 to 30 IBU.

For the hops, use a neutral bittering hop for most of the IBU. Put Zappa in the last 10 minutes of the boil at 15 g, in a 15 minute whirlpool at 80 °C at 30 g and as a dry hop at 40 g (2 g per litre).
The floor detail: split the batch

The best test of a strange hop is a split batch. Boil all of the wort together, with no Zappa in the boil. Divide it into two 10 litre fermenters. Dry hop one with 20 g of Zappa and the other with 20 g of a hop you know well, such as Strata or Olicana. Use the same yeast and the same temperature on the same day.

Taste at two weeks and at six. Note when the mint comes forward and when it fades. Mint-like notes often age differently from fruit, so the balance on day 14 may not match day 40.

If you are unsure, dose low. A first dry hop of 1 to 2 g per litre is enough to learn the character. On the next brew, double it in the whirlpool if you want more passion fruit, or hold it at the same level and move the dry hop earlier to reduce mint. Change one variable per batch and write it down. Our guide to dry hopping covers contact time and temperature.

Heavy dry hopping in a low-gravity beer also pulls out grassy flavours. Keep the base beer clean and a bit sturdy, with some body from wheat or oats, so the hop sits on something.

Stack the odd notes with care. A hop with a similar tropical edge, such as Moutere, reinforces the passion fruit and quiets the mint. A pine or dank hop makes the mint more medicinal. A soft citrus hop gives a brighter, more drinkable beer.

Food helps too. Mint pairs well with lamb, yoghurt dishes and fresh chutneys in Indian cooking. A Zappa pale ale can sit beside a mint raita or a seekh kebab without clashing. Treat that as a suggestion, not a rule.
Buying and storing it in India

Zappa is a specialist hop and may only turn up in small packs. Check the harvest year and buy foil packs flushed with inert gas. Freeze them. Thiol-type and volatile terpene aromas fade with warmth and oxygen. A pack that spent weeks on a warm shelf will taste of wet straw. If you cannot find it, brew the same recipe with a hop you can get and enjoy the process.

Learning to brew with an unusual hop is useful beyond the hop. It trains you to isolate a variable, taste blind and judge a change honestly. Those habits are what separate a homebrewer who produces a good beer by luck from one who can reproduce it. A structured brewing science course builds that discipline.
faqs: What does Zappa hop taste like?
Zappa is described with passion fruit and mint. Taste your own lot in a plain beer first to see how those notes balance.
How much Zappa should I dry hop with?
Start with 1 to 2 g per litre. Increase only after you have tasted the result. Too much can push the mint towards a toothpaste note.
Can I use Zappa in an IPA?
Yes, though it is easier to judge in a pale ale at 4.5% ABV. In a big IPA other hops can cover the mint.
